plural-suffix-men.title_tr: 们 (men) Plural Suffix (我们, 你们)
plural-suffix-men.intro_tr: 们 [men], in Chinese is a suffix added to the end of nouns or pronouns to indicate plurality; it functions similarly to the suffix "-lar/-ler" in Turkish. Fundamentally, it is used only with words that indicate HUMANS (我们, 你们, 他们, 老师们, 学生们, etc.); it is not normally used with animals or inanimate objects. If there is a specific number or quantity word before the noun (三个人, 很多学生, etc.), 们 is no longer necessary and is not used because plurality is already indicated by the number. At the HSK1 level, the most frequently encountered usage is the plural forms of personal pronouns: 我们[wǒmen], 你们[nǐmen], 他们/她们/它们[tāmen]. This lesson summarizes all the basic rules, exceptions, and common mistakes with 们 in table form.

you-have.intro_tr: 有[yǒu] is one of the most frequently used verbs in Chinese and has two basic meanings: "to have" (to have something/someone) and "to exist" (for something/someone to be present in a place). 有[yǒu] does not conjugate like regular verbs; it does not change with tense, person, or number, which is why it is easy to learn. The most important rule: 有[yǒu] is NEVER negated with 不[bù], but always with 没[méi] — this is one of the most confusing points for everyone learning Chinese. Additionally, when 有[yǒu] is used with the meaning of "to exist," the sentence order is very similar to the Turkish structure "there is X in place": Place + 有[yǒu] + Object.

ye-dou-adverbs.intro_tr: 也 [yě] and 都 [dōu] are two of the most frequently used adverbs in Chinese, and both always appear AFTER THE SUBJECT and BEFORE THE VERB or ADJECTIVE. 也 [yě] with the meaning 'also/too' conveys that the situation from the previous sentence is repeated (similarity/addition), while 都 [dōu] with the meaning 'all/everyone' indicates that a judgment applies to ALL elements that make up the subject; therefore, 都 [dōu] usually requires a plural or multi-element subject. These two adverbs are frequently used together (也都), and when combined with negation (都不 vs 不都), the meaning changes significantly — this is one of the most confusing points for HSK1 students. In the tables below, basic usage, positioning rules, order of combined use, negation differences, and common mistakes are listed in detail.

tables.caption_tr: 也 (yě) and 都 (dōu) — Basic Meanings and Functions
rows: Benzerlik/ekleme bildirir; bir önceki cümledeki durumun aynısının geçerli olduğunu belirtir

zai-preposition.title_tr: 在 (zài) Preposition: Expressing Location (在家吃饭)
zai-preposition.intro_tr: 在[zài] can be used both as a standalone verb meaning "to be in a place" and as a preposition to indicate WHERE an action takes place. When used as a preposition, the structure is generally Subject + 在[zài] + Place + Verb; that is, the phrase "在 + place" usually comes BEFORE the main verb, because we specify the location where the action takes place beforehand (在家吃饭 = "to eat at home", the action of eating takes place at home). In some verbs (especially resultative verbs like 住[zhù], 坐[zuò], 放[fàng], 生[shēng]) 在 comes AFTER the verb to indicate the place reached or arrived at as a result of the action. Mixing up these two usages is one of the most common mistakes made by Turkish-speaking students, which is why they are discussed separately in the tables below. Negation is always done with 不[bù] or 没[méi] before 在, never before the verb.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure of 在[zài] Preposition: Subject + 在 + Place + Verb
rows: Özne + 不/没 + 在 + Yer + Fiil
Zarf + 在 + Yer + Fiil (zaman önce gelir)

他们在饭馆吃饭。 (Tāmen zài fànguǎn chīfàn.) - Restoranda yemek yiyorlar.

孩子们在公园玩儿。 (Háizimen zài gōngyuán wánr.) - Çocuklar parkta oynuyor.

neng-can.title_tr: 能 (néng): 'Can/Be Able to' Expressing Physical Ability
neng-can.intro_tr: 能[néng] is an auxiliary verb (助动词[zhùdòngcí]) used to indicate that one has the PHYSICAL ABILITY, OBJECTIVE CONDITIONS (time, place, health status, rules, etc.), or POSSIBILITY necessary to perform an action. It means 'can/be able to, have the capacity, be possible'. It differs in meaning from 会[huì], which expresses a learned skill, and 可以[kěyǐ], which generally expresses possibility based on permission or rules, but in everyday conversation all three are often used interchangeably. 能[néng] always comes directly before the verb and never takes aspect markers like 了[le] or 过[guo]. The negative form is 不能[bù néng], and questions are formed by adding 吗[ma] or by using the alternation 能不能[néng bu néng].

ji-duoshao.intro_tr: 几[jǐ] and 多少[duōshao] are two basic question words in Çince meaning "how many, how many pieces" and both are used to ask numbers, but their usage rules differ. 几[jǐ] is generally used for numbers smaller than 10 that are predictable and must always be accompanied by a measure word (量词[liàngcí]): 几个[jǐ ge], 几本[jǐ běn], 几口[jǐ kǒu], etc. 多少[duōshao], on the other hand, can be used for any size number (small or large, unknown) and can be used directly before the noun without a measure word. This lesson summarizes the differences between 几[jǐ] and 多少[duōshao], common question patterns, and special cases (age, money, phone number, date/time) in tables.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Differences Between 几[jǐ] and 多少[duōshao]
rows: Evet, zorunlu: 几 + 量词 + 名词
Hayır, doğrudan isimle kullanılabilir (ölçü sözcüğü isteğe bağlı)
Saat, tarih, yaş (çocuk), aile üyesi sayısı, sınıf/oda no.
Para, telefon numarası, nüfus, uzun/büyük sayılar
Sınır yok, çok büyük sayılar da olabilir

he-conjunction.intro_tr: 和 [hé] is one of the most basic and frequently used conjunctions in Chinese; it means 'and' or 'with' in Turkish. Its primary function is to connect two or more NOUNS, PRONOUNS, or NOUN PHRASES to each other (for example 'apple and banana', 'you and me'). 和 has an important difference from the English word 'and': it is not used to connect VERBS or SENTENCES — for this purpose other structures such as 也, 还, 然后 are used. Additionally, 和 can appear before a noun and function as a postposition (preposition) meaning 'together with'; in this usage it is almost identical to 跟 [gēn]. At HSK1 level, the two most frequently encountered functions of 和 are: (1) connecting nouns and (2) usage as a postposition 'with' before a verb.

tones-basics.title_tr: Four Tones and Neutral Tone (四声与轻声)
tones-basics.intro_tr: Chinese is a tonal language (声调 / shēngdiào); when the same syllable is pronounced with a different tone, it takes on a completely different meaning — therefore, tone is the most fundamental building block of learning Chinese. Standard Mandarin Chinese has four main tones and, in addition to these, an unstressed/lightly pronounced 'neutral tone' (轻声 / qīngshēng). Tones are indicated in pinyin writing by diacritical marks placed above vowels (ā á ǎ à); in the neutral tone, no mark is used. A student starting from zero level must first correctly hear and mimic the pitch curve (pitch contour) of each tone, then learn the rules for placing tone marks and where the neutral tone is used. The tables below summarize these four tones, tone mark rules, the neutral tone, and common mistakes.

de-possession.intro_tr: 的[de] is one of the most frequently used particles in Chinese and has two basic functions: first, to express possession (ownership) — it is like the equivalent of the Turkish "-in/-ın" suffix; second, to modify a noun with an adjective or another noun, answering the question "which...?". The general pattern is: [Possessor / Modifier] + 的[de] + [Noun]. However, with single-syllable adjectives and very close family/relationship nouns, 的[de] is often dropped. Also, 的[de], if the noun following it is understood from context, can be completely omitted and used in its place (e.g., 我的 = "mine"). This page summarizes all the basic usage patterns and exceptions of 的[de] in table form.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Pattern: Pronoun + 的[de] + Noun (Possession)
footnotes_tr: Pattern: [Possessor] + 的[de] + [Possessed Thing]. It is the exact equivalent of the Turkish possessive suffix ('-in/-ın').

tables.caption_tr: Noun + 的[de] + Noun (Belonging / Relationship Expression)
footnotes_tr: Here, 的[de] between two nouns adds the meaning 'of / belonging to': A的[de]B = 'A's B'.

tables.caption_tr: Adjective + 的[de] + Noun: When Is 的[de] Used, When Is It Not?
rows: 红花 [hóng huā] — kırmızı çiçek; 好人 [hǎo rén] — iyi insan
漂亮的花 [piàoliang de huā] — güzel çiçek
很/非常 gibi zarfla pekiştirilmiş sıfat
很好的朋友 [hěn hǎo de péngyou] — çok iyi bir arkadaş
红色的衣服 [hóngsè de yīfu] — kırmızı renkli kıyafet
footnotes_tr: General rule: the longer/more emphatic the adjective, the more necessary 的[de] is.

tables.caption_tr: When Is 的[de] Dropped? (Close Relationship / Family Exceptions)
rows: Aile üyeleri genelde 的[de] almadan da doğaldır
我的手机 [wǒ de shǒujī] — telefonum

footnotes_tr: For concrete, possessible objects (book, phone, car), 的[de] is almost always required; for connections with people/institutions, it is optional.

negation-bu.intro_tr: 不 [bù] is the most basic and most frequently used negation word in Chinese; placed BEFORE verbs, adjectives, and auxiliary verbs, it conveys the meaning "is not, does not do, will not do." It is used to negate general truths, habits, future intentions, desires, and situation-describing sentences; however, for COMPLETED past actions, 没 (méi) is preferred instead. Standing alone, 不 is pronounced with the 4th tone (bù), but when immediately followed by a syllable with the 4th tone, it changes to the 2nd tone (bú) — this is the most important tone rule that must be memorized at the HSK1 level. On this page, the position of 不, tone changes, its inability to be used with 有, and common mistakes are summarized in table form.

tables.caption_tr: 不 [bù] Tone Change Rule
rows: 去不去？—不。[qù bu qù? — bù.]
footnotes_tr: Tone change affects only pronunciation (speech); in writing, the character is always 不; when writing pinyin, the changed tone is marked (bú).

question-words.title_tr: Question Words: 什么 (shénme), 谁 (shéi), 哪儿 (nǎr), 怎么 (zěnme)
question-words.intro_tr: In Chinese, question words (疑问代词) are not moved to the beginning of the sentence like in Turkish and English; the questioned element stays in its normal place in the sentence, which is called "in-situ" questioning (in-situ). In other words, the sentence structure is exactly the same as a statement sentence; only the unknown element is replaced with a question word. 什么[shénme] "what", 谁[shéi] "who", 哪儿[nǎr] "where", 怎么[zěnme] "how/why" are the four basic question words, and derivatives like 为什么, 怎么样, 哪, 几, 多少, 多+adjective are added to them. In these types of questions, the particle 吗 is not added to the end of the sentence — 吗 is only used in yes/no questions. The tables below summarize all question words, their patterns, and common mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Question Words (什么, 谁, 哪儿, 怎么) and Their Derivatives
rows: 你喝什么? [Nǐ hē shénme?] — Ne içiyorsun?

ne-question.title_tr: 呢 (ne) Particle: "What About You?" Type Elliptical Questions
ne-question.intro_tr: The 呢[ne] particle is one of the most frequently encountered sentence-final particles at HSK1 level and is used to form elliptical questions meaning "what about you? what about him/her/it? what about this?" After discussing a topic, to ask the same question for another person, object, or topic without reformulating the complete sentence, the pattern "noun/pronoun + 呢" is used; this is very similar to the Turkish expressions "what about you?" or "but what about...?". 呢 can also be used when asking about the location of something/someone in the sense of "Where is X?" (e.g., 我的手机呢? "Where is my phone?"). Additionally, it appears in the pattern 在/正在 + verb + 呢 to emphasize the present tense, but this lesson specifically focuses on "what about you?" type elliptical questions. In questions formed with 呢, context is very important; because this same short pattern is merely repeating the question asked in the previous sentence, without adding a new verb.

tables.caption_tr: Elliptical Question Structure with 呢: Noun/Pronoun + 呢?
rows: 我们要走了，你们呢[nǐmen ne]？
这个太贵了，那个呢[nàge ne]？
我喜欢中国菜，日本菜呢[Rìběn cài ne]？
Ben Çin yemeğini severim, ya Japon yemeği?
footnotes_tr: In these types of questions formed with 呢, the verb is not repeated; the question is understood from the context of the previous sentence.
This structure can only be used when the conversational context is clear; it does not carry meaning by itself.

rows: 我的书呢[wǒ de shū ne]？

footnotes_tr: The main focus of this lesson is the 'elliptical question' usage in the first line; the others are provided for comparison purposes.

footnotes_tr: 呢 does not form a complete yes/no question; it only briefly repeats a question that was asked before.
吗 always forms a complete and independent interrogative sentence and does not require context.

measure-word-ge.intro_tr: 个[gè] is the most common and most 'general-purpose' measure word in Chinese (量词[liàngcí]). When counting a noun in Chinese, a measure word must always be used before the noun; it is similar to structures in Turkish like 'bir tane elma, iki kişi' but in Chinese it is almost mandatory in every count. 个[gè] is used especially for counting people, general objects, and many nouns without a clearly defined shape; when you don't know which measure word to use, 个[gè] is usually the safest choice. The basic pattern is: Number + 个[gè] + Noun. It is also frequently used together with demonstrative and interrogative words like 这[zhè], 那[nà], 哪[nǎ] (这个[zhège], 那个[nàge], 哪个[nǎge]). In normal speech, 个[gè] is usually pronounced with a light/neutral tone (轻声[qīngshēng]).

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: Number + 个[gè] + Noun
rows: kaç öğrenci? (多少 ile 个 çoğu zaman düşer)
footnotes_tr: '一' (one) when it comes before a measure word usually changes from the fourth tone to the second tone: 一个 → yí gè.
'两' (liǎng) is used instead of '二' (èr) meaning 'two' before measure words: 两个 (two), one never says 二个.

tables.caption_tr: 个[gè] with Demonstrative and Interrogative Words
footnotes_tr: After 这个/那个/哪个, a noun may not be spoken; it is understood from context (like 'this one, that one' in Turkish).

footnotes_tr: Practical tip for beginners: If you can't remember the correct measure word, using 个 is usually understandable, but at an advanced level it is important to learn the correct measure words.

yao-want.title_tr: 要 (yào): Wanting, Necessity, and Near Future
yao-want.intro_tr: 要 [yào] is one of the most frequently used verbs in Chinese and carries three different meanings depending on context: (1) when used with a noun, it means "to want" (我要咖啡 - I want coffee), (2) when used with a verb, it means "to want to do" or "must do" (我要学习 - I need to study/I want to study), (3) when used at the end of a sentence with 了 [le], it describes something that will happen in the near future: "要...了" (要下雨了 - It will rain). The most important trap is that the negation of 要 changes depending on the meaning: for the meaning of wanting, use 不想 [bùxiǎng], for the meaning of obligation, use 不用 [búyòng] or 不必 [búbì], and for prohibition/command, use 不要 [búyào] — 不要 never directly means "I don't want," it means "don't do it!" On this page you will find all the uses of 要, its negative forms, and how it differs from similar modal verbs in tables.

hanzi-strokes-radicals.title_tr: Hanzi Fundamentals: Stroke Order and Radicals
hanzi-strokes-radicals.intro_tr: Chinese characters (汉字[hànzì]) are not randomly drawn shapes, but are composed of specific "strokes" (笔画[bǐhuà]) units and a fixed writing order (笔顺[bǐshùn]). Each character also contains a "radical" (部首[bùshǒu]); this is typically a small component that indicates the character's semantic domain (water, fire, person, hand, etc.) and is also the basis for looking up characters in a dictionary. Writing with the correct stroke order is not just aesthetic; it also makes it easier to remember the character and speed up handwriting. This page summarizes, in tabular form, the basic stroke types, universal stroke order rules, the most common radicals, and character structure types for students starting from zero.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Stroke Types (基本笔画[jīběn bǐhuà])

Sol üstten sağ alta inen eğik çizgi
Küçük nokta, sağ alta doğru bırakılır
Sol alttan sağ üste kalkan kısa çizgi
Yatay çizgi, sonra dik aşağı dönüş

Önce dış, sonra iç, en son kapak
Kuşatan çerçeve önce, içerik sonra, alt kapanış en son
口'nun üst+yanları → içerik(玉) → alt çizgi kapatılır
Ortadaki dikey/nokta önce, sonra sağ-sol simetrik parçalar
Yarı kuşatmalı karakterlerde önce iç yazılır, kapatma çizgisi en son
üst+sol çerçeve → içerik → alt kapama çizgisi
Yatay çizgi çoğunlukla en üstte başlar
Üst üste yatay çizgiler varsa en üsttekinden başlanır
üst 横 → orta 横 → 竖 → alt 横

basic-word-order.intro_tr: In Chinese, the basic sentence word order differs from Turkish in that it follows Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) structure; that is, the verb comes before the object. Whereas in Turkish when you say "I eat apple", the order is Subject-Object-Verb (SOV), in Chinese it is written as 我[wǒ]吃[chī]苹果[píngguǒ], meaning "I eat apple" (Subject-Verb-Object). This is the most basic and most critical grammar rule to learn at HSK1 level because all future sentence structures are built on this skeleton. Time and place expressions, on the other hand, come BEFORE the verb, usually right after the subject — this is also a different logic from Turkish. Thoroughly internalizing the patterns on this page will establish a solid foundation for understanding advanced Chinese structures.

tables.caption_tr: Basic SVO Structure: Subject + Verb (Predicate) + Object
footnotes_tr: This is the most basic skeleton of a Chinese sentence. In sentences without an object, only Subject + Verb is used (e.g., 我睡觉[wǒ shuìjiào] - I sleep).

tables.caption_tr: Extended Sentence Order: Subject + Time + Place + Adverb + Verb + Object
footnotes_tr: The order is fixed: first TIME, then PLACE, then ADVERB, finally VERB and OBJECT. This order cannot be changed.
The time word can also come at the beginning of the sentence (before the subject): 今天我在学校学习汉语[Jīntiān wǒ zài xuéxiào xuéxí Hànyǔ].

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Turkish (SOV) and Chinese (SVO) Sentence Word Order
footnotes_tr: Because of this fundamental difference, Turkish students typically tend to place the verb at the end of the sentence — this is incorrect in Chinese and distorts the meaning.

tables.caption_tr: Frequent Word Order Errors and Corrections
rows: Çince'de fiil her zaman nesneden önce gelir, Türkçe alışkanlığıyla sona atılmamalıdır.
＊我吃苹果今天。[Wǒ chī píngguǒ jīntiān.]
我今天吃苹果。[Wǒ jīntiān chī píngguǒ.]
Zaman sözcüğü fiilden önce, genelde öznenin hemen ardından gelmelidir.
＊我学习在学校。[Wǒ xuéxí zài xuéxiào.]
我在学校学习。[Wǒ zài xuéxiào xuéxí.]
在+yer ifadesi genel kural olarak fiilden önce gelir (住[zhù] gibi bazı fiiller istisnadır: 我住在北京[Wǒ zhù zài Běijīng]).
Sıfatlar doğrudan yüklem olabilir; 是[shì] sadece isim cümlelerinde kullanılır.
我今天都去。[Wǒ jīntiān dōu qù.]
Zarflar (都, 也, 不 vb.) her zaman fiilin hemen önünde bulunur.

tables.caption_tr: SVO Structure with Special Verbs (是, 有, 在)
rows: 我有一本书。[Wǒ yǒu yì běn shū.]
footnotes_tr: These verbs also follow the SVO pattern; only the 'object' part can be a noun, place, or surname.

zai-location-verb.intro_tr: The 在 (zài) verb is used to express where a person or thing is located and means "to be in/at" in Turkish (-de/-da bulunmak, olmak). The basic sentence structure is Subject + 在 + Place; after 在 there must be a place/location expression, other types of words (adjectives, nouns, etc.) cannot come directly. To make it negative, 不 (bù) is usually added before 在 (不在); when describing not being somewhere in the past, 没 (méi) can also be used. 在 is also used as a preposition (在 preposition) that comes before another verb and indicates where the action takes place — these two usage patterns are often confused at HSK1 level, so the difference between them is shown separately.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: Affirmative, Negative, and Question Sentences
rows: Soru (吗): Özne + 在 + Yer + 吗？
Olumlu-Olumsuz Soru: Özne + 在不在 + Yer？
footnotes_tr: 不 (bù) is normally in the 4th tone, but when a 4th tone syllable follows it (like 在 zài), it changes to the 2nd tone and is read as 'bú': 不在 → bú zài.

tables.caption_tr: Using 在 with Frequently Used Place Words
rows: 我在家。(Wǒ zài jiā.) — Ben evdeyim.
他在学校。(Tā zài xuéxiào.) — O okulda.
她在公司。(Tā zài gōngsī.) — O şirkette.
书在这儿。(Shū zài zhèr.) — Kitap burada.
他在那儿。(Tā zài nàr.) — O orada.
你在哪儿？(Nǐ zài nǎr?) — Sen neredesin?
我在图书馆。(Wǒ zài túshūguǎn.) — Ben kütüphanedeyim.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of 在 (Verb: 'to be located') and 在 (Preposition: place marking)
rows: 他在图书馆。(Tā zài túshūguǎn.) — O kütüphanede(dir).
Cümlede başka bir fiil yoktur; 在 tek başına 'bulunmak' anlamındaki ana fiildir.
他在图书馆看书。(Tā zài túshūguǎn kàn shū.) — O kütüphanede kitap okuyor.
在 burada eylemin gerçekleştiği yeri gösteren bir edattır; asıl fiil 看书'dur.
footnotes_tr: To distinguish these two usages: if there is another verb (action) after 在 in the sentence, then 在 is a preposition; otherwise, 在 itself is a verb.

tables.caption_tr: Using 在 Together with Adverbs
rows: 我也在家。(Wǒ yě zài jiā.)
他们都在教室。(Tāmen dōu zài jiàoshì.)
他还在公司。(Tā hái zài gōngsī.)
她一直在图书馆。(Tā yìzhí zài túshūguǎn.)
footnotes_tr: Adverbs always come before 在, never between 在 and the place word: 他都在家 (correct) not *他在都家 (incorrect).

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes

meiyou-negation.title_tr: 没有 (méiyǒu): Not Having and Not Having Done
meiyou-negation.intro_tr: 没有[méiyǒu] is a very useful negation word in Chinese with two basic functions: it is both the only negative form of the 有[yǒu] verb ("to have, to exist") and indicates actions that did not occur in the past or have not yet been completed ("I didn't do it, he didn't come"). In spoken language, it is often shortened and used simply as 没[méi]; both forms are valid. Unlike 不[bù], 没有 negates completed/past events and is not used together with 了[le]. Additionally, it is also used for making comparisons in the pattern "A 没有 B + adjective" with the meaning "A is not as ... as B".

tables.caption_tr: The three basic uses of 没有[méiyǒu]
rows: 他没有我高。[Tā méiyǒu wǒ gāo.]
footnotes_tr: In comparative structures, only 没 should not be used; the complete form 没有 is preferred.

tables.caption_tr: The difference between 没(有)[méi(yǒu)] and 不[bù]
rows: 有 ile birlikte kullanılmaz (*不有 yanlış)
不...了 mümkündür (durum değişikliği: 我不去了)

tables.caption_tr: Shortened and inflected forms of 没有[méiyǒu]
rows: Yazı dilinde ve vurgu istendiğinde tercih edilir.
Günlük konuşmada çok yaygın, anlam aynıdır.
Her iki form da doğru ve eşdeğerdir.
我没(有)去过中国。[Wǒ méi(yǒu) qùguo Zhōngguó.]
有 konuşma dilinde sıklıkla düşer, sadece 没 kalır.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently used 没有[méiyǒu] patterns

hiç yok, bir damla bile yok

没关系，别担心。[Méi guānxi, bié dānxīn.]

ma-question.intro_tr: 吗[ma] is the most basic and most common way to form yes/no questions in Chinese. It is added to the end of any affirmative sentence without changing the word order at all; in other words, the pattern "Subject + Predicate + 吗?" is sufficient. 吗[ma] is always read with a NEUTRAL tone and comes at the very end of the sentence, just before the punctuation mark. This particle is NOT used in sentences containing question words (such as 什么, 谁, 哪儿, 怎么) and is not used together with the V不V (affirmative-negative) structure — these already form questions on their own. Since it is one of the most basic grammar points of HSK1 level, it is important to learn its correct position and correct usage conditions well.

tables.caption_tr: Forming Question Sentences with 吗[ma]: Basic Structure (Affirmative Sentence + 吗)
rows: 你是学生吗？[Nǐ shì xuésheng ma?]
他去学校吗？[Tā qù xuéxiào ma?]
你喜欢猫吗？[Nǐ xǐhuan māo ma?]
这是你的书。[Zhè shì nǐ de shū.]
这是你的书吗？[Zhè shì nǐ de shū ma?]
Meşgul müsün? (吗 ile 很 genelde düşer)
你有时间吗？[Nǐ yǒu shíjiān ma?]
footnotes_tr: When 吗[ma] is added, the word order in the sentence does NOT change at all; only 吗 is added to the end of the sentence.
Adverbs of degree such as 很[hěn] are generally not used in 吗 question sentences or may remain for emphasis purposes; it does not create a difference in meaning.

tables.caption_tr: Patterns for Answering 吗 Questions
rows: 你是老师吗？[Nǐ shì lǎoshī ma?]
是，我是老师。[Shì, wǒ shì lǎoshī.]
不是，我不是老师。[Bú shì, wǒ bú shì lǎoshī.]
你喜欢咖啡吗？[Nǐ xǐhuan kāfēi ma?]
喜欢，我喜欢咖啡。[Xǐhuan, wǒ xǐhuan kāfēi.]
不喜欢，我不喜欢咖啡。[Bù xǐhuan, wǒ bù xǐhuan kāfēi.]
你有时间吗？[Nǐ yǒu shíjiān ma?]
有，我有时间。[Yǒu, wǒ yǒu shíjiān.]
没有，我没有时间。[Méiyǒu, wǒ méiyǒu shíjiān.]
你去过中国吗？[Nǐ qùguo Zhōngguó ma?]
没去过，我没去过。[Méi qùguo, wǒ méi qùguo.]
忙，我很忙。[Máng, wǒ hěn máng.]
不忙，我不忙。[Bù máng, wǒ bù máng.]
footnotes_tr: Unlike in Turkish, 'yes/no' is not answered with a single word; generally, the verb/adjective in the question is repeated, using 是/不是, 有/没有, or the relevant verb/adjective + 不.
The negative of the verb 有[yǒu] is always 没[méi], not 不[bù]: 没有, never 不有 is used.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of 吗 with Other Question Structures
rows: Nötr, basit evet/hayır sorusu; en yaygın ve tarafsız biçim
你忙不忙？[Nǐ máng bu máng?]
吗 ile AYNI anlam ama farklı biçim; 吗 ile BİRLİKTE kullanılmaz
我很好，你呢？[Wǒ hěn hǎo, nǐ ne?]
Önceki cümleye bağlı kısaltılmış soru; 吗 gibi bağımsız soru kurmaz
Konuşmacının zaten bir tahmini/varsayımı vardır, 吗'dan daha az kesin
Soru sözcüğü zaten soru anlamı verir; 吗 EKLENMEZ

吗 bir cümlede sadece BİR KEZ kullanılır
你不喜欢猫吗？ (olumsuz cümle + 吗 hatalı sanılır)
你不喜欢猫吗？ (bu aslında DOĞRU!)
Olumsuz cümleler de 吗 alabilir: 'Kedileri sevmiyor musun?' anlamı doğrudur, hata değildir

time-word-position.title_tr: Location of Time Words (今天[jīntiān] 我去...)
time-word-position.intro_tr: In Chinese, time words (今天[jīntiān] 'today', 明天[míngtiān] 'tomorrow', 三点[sān diǎn] 'three o'clock' and similar) are positioned, unlike Turkish and English, not at the END of the sentence but BEFORE the PREDICATE. The time word can be placed either immediately after the subject, or at the very beginning of the sentence if emphasis is desired, even before the subject — but it can never come after the verb or object. This rule applies to "time POINTS" (今天, 三点, 星期一 etc.) that determine "when"; "time COMPLEMENTS" (三年, 两个小时 etc.) that determine "how long" work in the opposite way, coming AFTER the verb. When multiple time words are used consecutively, the order is always from largest to smallest: year → month → day → day of the week → hour. This is a simple but one of the most frequently misplaced rules by Turkish students, because in the native language time expressions are generally added at the end of the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Word Order: Where Does the Time Word Go?
rows: 我今天去学校。[Wǒ jīntiān qù xuéxiào.]  (Ben bugün okula gidiyorum.)
En yaygın ve nötr dizilim. Zaman sözcüğü özneden hemen sonra, fiilden önce gelir.
今天我去学校。[Jīntiān wǒ qù xuéxiào.]  (Bugün ben okula gidiyorum.)
Zaman vurgulanmak istendiğinde veya cümle bir zaman diliminden bahsederek başlıyorsa, zaman sözcüğü cümle başına, öznenin önüne de gelebilir. Anlam değişmez, sadece vurgu kayar.
YANLIŞ! Türkçe/İngilizce alışkanlığıyla zaman sözcüğünü cümle sonuna koymak Çincede büyük bir gramer hatasıdır.
他昨天没有来。[Tā zuótiān méiyǒu lái.]  (O dün gelmedi.)
不[bù] / 没(有)[méi(yǒu)] olumsuzluk sözcükleri zaman sözcüğünden SONRA, fiilden hemen önce yer alır.

tables.caption_tr: Difference Between Time Point (When?) and Duration Complement (How Long?)
rows: Zaman noktası (今天, 三点, 星期一...)
我三点去。[Wǒ sān diǎn qù.]
Süre tümleci (三年, 两个小时, 五天...)
我学了三年汉语。[Wǒ xuéle sān nián Hànyǔ.]
Zaman noktası önce, süre fiilden sonra
我昨天等了他两个小时。[Wǒ zuótiān děngle tā liǎng ge xiǎoshí.]
footnotes_tr: For the topic of duration complements, see the separate 'Duration Complement' grammar page.

tables.caption_tr: Ordering in Multiple Time Expressions (From Largest to Smallest)
footnotes_tr: Full example: 2024年7月18号星期五下午三点 [èr líng èr sì nián qī yuè shíbā hào xīngqīwǔ xiàwǔ sān diǎn] — In Turkish the order is exactly the opposite (hour, day, month, year), which is why this is the most important difference to pay attention to.

tables.caption_tr: Co-occurrence of Time and Location Words
rows: 我今天在家休息。[Wǒ jīntiān zài jiā xiūxi.]  (Bugün evde dinleniyorum.)
明天我们在公园见面。[Míngtiān wǒmen zài gōngyuán jiànmiàn.]  (Yarın parkta buluşuyoruz.)
footnotes_tr: Rule: Time always comes BEFORE the location word. Order: Subject + Time + Location + Verb + Object.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Time Words
Common Mistakes
rows: Türkçe alışkanlığıyla zaman sözcüğü cümle sonuna konmuş; Çincede bu yer fiilden öncedir.
Olumsuzluk eki zaman sözcüğünden önce değil, sonra gelmelidir.
✅ 我们下午三点见面。 / 下午三点我们见面。
Zaman birimleri kendi içinde büyükten küçüğe sıralanmalıdır (下午 önce, 三点 sonra).
Zaman sözcüğü yer sözcüğünden (在家) önce gelmelidir.

examples.note_tr: The time word 今天[jīntiān] comes after the subject and before the predicate (adjectival verb).

examples.target: 他昨天没有来学校。

personal-pronouns.title_tr: Personal Pronouns: 我 (wǒ) / 你 (nǐ) / 他·她·它 (tā)
personal-pronouns.intro_tr: In Chinese, personal pronouns are much simpler compared to Turkish: verbs are not conjugated according to person, and learning a single pronoun list is sufficient. Singular pronouns are 我[wǒ] (I), 你[nǐ] (you) and 他/她/它[tā] (he/she/it); when speaking about the third singular person, it is always pronounced with the same "tā" sound, but only in writing different characters are used for male (他), female (她) and inanimate/animal (它) — therefore during speech, gender distinction is not heard, only seen in text. To make plural, the suffix 们[men] is added to the end of the pronoun (我们, 你们, 他们/她们/它们). The respectful/formal equivalent of the pronoun 你[nǐ] is 您[nín] and it is preferred when addressing elders, foreigners or customers. For "we" there is also 咱们[zánmen]; this is an intimate conversational form that emphasizes including the listener definitively in "we".

hen-adjective-predicate.title_tr: 很 (hěn) + Adjective Predicate — 是 Not Used
hen-adjective-predicate.intro_tr: In Chinese, adjectives (形容词[xíngróngcí]) can be used directly as predicates, and in this usage, 是[shì], which corresponds to the verb 'to be' in English/Turkish, IS NOT USED — that is, the sentence "She is beautiful" is not 她是漂亮, but is constructed as 她很漂亮[tā hěn piàoliang]. Generally, 很[hěn] is placed before the adjective predicate; this 很 often does not carry the meaning of "very", but is rather a grammatical particle that provides natural balance to the sentence (which is why it is also called "empty 很"). If a bare adjective is used without 很 (e.g., 她漂亮), the sentence implies a comparison or contrast and generally sounds odd/incomplete. In negative sentences, 不[bù] or 不太[bú tài] is used instead of 很; in interrogative sentences, 很 is completely dropped and 吗[ma] or adjective-不-adjective (similar to V-不-V) structure is preferred. This structure is one of the most fundamental and frequently encountered grammar points of HSK1 level.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: Subject + 很 + Adjective (是 NOT PRESENT)
footnotes_tr: Note: Sentences like 我是好 or 天气是热 are INCORRECT. 是 is used only in noun predicates (我是学生[wǒ shì xuésheng]).

xiang-want.title_tr: 想 [xiǎng]: To want, To miss, To think
xiang-want.intro_tr: 想 [xiǎng] is a verb frequently used in Chinese that appears with three different meanings: "to want" (to desire doing something), "to miss" (to long for a person/place), and "to think" (to ponder a topic or express an opinion). Its most common usage is appearing before another verb to express personal desire and intention: 想 + Verb structure means "...-want to". 想 differs semantically from other auxiliary verbs like 要 [yào] and 会 [huì]/能 [néng]; therefore, it is necessary to distinguish the differences between them well. Its negation is usually done with 不 [bù] (不想), not with 没 [méi], because 想 expresses a desire/intention, not a completed action.

tables.caption_tr: Three Basic Meanings of the Verb 想 [xiǎng]
rows: Wǒ xiǎng tā bú huì lái.
footnotes_tr: Which meaning is intended can be understood from context: if before a verb, it means 'to want', if before a noun it usually means 'to miss', if at the beginning of a sentence expressing an opinion, it means 'to think/suppose'.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Patterns with 想 (Affirmative / Negative / Question)
rows: Nǐ xiǎng bu xiǎng qù Běijīng?
Pekin'e gitmek istiyor musun, istemiyor musun?
Wǒ xiǎng qù Běijīng, nǐ ne?
Ben Pekin'e gitmek istiyorum, ya sen?
footnotes_tr: In the V不V question form, 想 is not repeated twice; just '想不想' is sufficient, followed by the complete verb expression.
Since 想 is an emotional/desire-based verb, it can be strengthened with degree adverbs (很, 非常, 真).

tables.caption_tr: 想 vs 要 vs 会 vs 能: Comparison
footnotes_tr: 想 usually expresses a polite wish, while 要 carries a more direct and sometimes commanding request meaning.
Both 想 and 要 can be used for a future action, but 想 is less certain/definite.

tables.caption_tr: Negation: The Difference Between 不想 vs 没想(到)
rows: Wǒ méi xiǎngdào tā huì lái.
footnotes_tr: Since 想 expresses a desire/intention, its normal negation is with 不, because 没 is generally used to negate completed actions.
没想到 is a fixed expression and means 'not to expect, not to anticipate'; there is no such usage as 不想到.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Fixed Expressions with 想
rows: Wǒ xiǎng tā jīntiān bù lái le.
footnotes_tr: Structures like 想起来 and 想不到 are advanced patterns where 想 combines with directional/resultative complements to acquire different meanings; it is sufficient to recognize them at the beginner level.

demonstratives-zhe-na.intro_tr: 这 [zhè] "this" and 那 [nà] "that" are the most basic demonstrative words in Chinese; 这 is used for objects/places/situations close to the speaker, and 那 is used for those far away. They can stand alone as subject or modifier, but if they are used before a noun, a measure word (量词) must necessarily be inserted between them — unlike separate words in Turkish like "this" and "a", in Chinese the pattern 这/那 + measure word + noun is mandatory. Many derivatives are formed from these two root words, such as location (这儿/那儿), manner (这么/那么), appearance (这样/那样), and plural (这些/那些). At HSK1 level, 这个 [zhège] and 那个 [nàge] are most frequently used; 个 [ge] here is a general-purpose measure word.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Forms of the 这 (zhè) and 那 (nà) Family
rows: bu kadar, böyle / o kadar, öyle
bu şekilde, böyle / o şekilde, öyle
footnotes_tr: 个 [ge] in fast speech is generally pronounced with a neutral tone: 这个 → zhège, 那个 → nàge.
这儿/那儿 are used more in Northern Chinese (Beijing dialect) in spoken language, while 这里/那里 are used in every region and in written language.

tables.caption_tr: 这/那 + Measure Word + Noun Pattern
footnotes_tr: After the plural forms 这些/那些, a measure word is NOT additionally used; uses like 这些个 are incorrect.
If a number is specified, the measure word comes before the number: 这两本书 [zhè liǎng běn shū] 'this two CL book'.

shi-copula.intro_tr: 是[shì] in Chinese means "to be" and is the basic copula (linking verb) that links two nouns to each other; it serves the function of the "-dır/-dir" suffix in Turkish. The structure is very simple: Subject + 是[shì] + Noun. 是[shì] is never conjugated according to person, tense, or number — it remains the same for all subjects, and this makes Chinese grammar much easier compared to Turkish. The most common mistake is trying to use 是[shì] with adjectives as well; however, in Chinese, 是[shì] is NOT USED in adjective predicates, instead an adverb like 很[hěn] is used. On this page, the affirmative, negative, and question forms of 是[shì] and the most common usage patterns are summarized in table form.

tables.caption_tr: 是[shì]'s Conjugation for All Subjects (Invariable!)
footnotes_tr: 是[shì] is never conjugated with suffixes like -le/-lar, -sınız; it remains the same for all persons and numbers.
Tense does not change 是[shì]: the same 是[shì] is used for past, present, and future, and tense is generally indicated with a separate time word (昨天, 明天 etc.).

tables.caption_tr: Affirmative, Negative, and Question Structures
rows: Bú shì, wǒ bú shì xuéshēng.
footnotes_tr: 不[bù] is normally read with the 4th tone, but before 是[shì] (4th tone) it is pronounced like the second tone: 不是 → bú shì.
In the 是不是 question, 是 is not repeated twice; only the 是不是 pattern is used, and it should not be confused with 是吗.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistake: 是[shì] or 很[hěn]?
rows: 很 nötr vurgu taşır, 'çok' anlamı zayıflar
这个苹果很甜。(Zhège píngguǒ hěn tián.)
footnotes_tr: In Chinese, adjectives can already function as predicates (Subject + Adjective), so 是 is not placed between them; 很 performs a linking function and generally does not carry the emphasis of 'very'.
If one wants to really express the meaning of 'very', adverbs like 太 (tài) or 非常 (fēicháng) are preferred: 非常高 (fēicháng gāo) = very tall.

tables.caption_tr: 是[shì]'s Common Usage Areas
footnotes_tr: 是[shì] usually links two noun phrases to each other; after it comes a noun (or noun phrase), not an adjective or verb.

names-jiao-xing.intro_tr: 叫[jiào] and 姓[xìng] are two fundamental verbs used in Chinese to introduce oneself or others, and they come directly after the subject like "be called / be surnamed" in English; 是[shì] is never inserted between them. 姓[xìng] is used ONLY to indicate surname (我姓王 = My surname is Wang), while 叫[jiào] can be used to state both the full name and just the first name (我叫王小明 or 我叫小明 both are correct). In Chinese, the naming order is the reverse of Turkish: surname comes first (姓), then given name (名字) — 王小明 = Wang (surname) + Xiaoming (given name). In polite/formal contexts, the formula 您贵姓？[Nín guìxìng?] is used to ask for a surname; 什么[shénme] is never added to this formula. These structures are among the most fundamental greeting sentences at HSK1 level and constantly appear in daily conversation.

Tam ad VEYA sadece ad söylemek için

İkisi de doğrudur: tam adla ya da sadece adla kullanılabilir.
Soyadı ve tam adı birlikte belirtmek için

tai-le.intro_tr: The 太...了 (tài...le) pattern is one of the most basic and most frequently encountered degree patterns in Chinese used to emphasize that an adjective or state is "excessive, too much, more than necessary." The structure is very simple: 太 (tài) comes before the adjective, and 了 (le) comes at the end of the sentence, forming the pattern "太 + Adjective + 了". This pattern can be used in two different emotional tones: to express a complaint/negativity ("too expensive, I can't afford it") or to express strong admiration/satisfaction ("so beautiful!", "wonderful!"). The 了 in this pattern does not carry a past tense meaning; it is only a particle that reinforces the exaggerated emphasis of the degree and is used almost always in spoken language, sometimes omitted in formal writing. It is important not to confuse this pattern with other degree adverbs like 很 (hěn), 非常 (fēicháng), and with its negative form 不太 (bù tài).

hui-can.intro_tr: 会 [huì] verb is one of the most basic auxiliary verbs of HSK1 level and conveys the meaning of having a skill acquired through learning, namely "knowing how to do / being able to do". For example, skills acquired later such as speaking a language, driving a car, swimming, cooking food are expressed with 会. 会 always comes BEFORE a verb and is used with the pattern "会 + verb"; its negative form is 不会 [bú huì]. Furthermore, 会 has another important meaning: indicating a situation that is likely to occur in the future ("... may occur, ... will occur"). On this page, the usage of 会 in the meaning of skill, its difference from 能 and 可以, and all conjugation patterns are covered in detail.

greetings-politeness.title_tr: Greetings and Polite Expressions (你好, 谢谢, 请, 对不起)
greetings-politeness.intro_tr: In Chinese, the most frequently used words in daily life are greetings and polite expressions; these are basic patterns that should be learned even before constructing sentences. Expressions such as 你好[nǐhǎo] "hello", 谢谢[xièxie] "thank you", 请[qǐng] "please" and 对不起[duìbuqǐ] "I'm sorry" are fixed patterns that can be used independently and are usually paired with a specific response (谢谢 → 不客气, 对不起 → 没关系, etc.). The distinction between formal/informal versions of these expressions is also important: 您好[nínhǎo] for elders and formal settings, while 你好[nǐhǎo] can be used with anyone. This page summarizes all basic polite expressions at HSK level 1, from greetings that change hourly throughout the day to the correct responses for requests and apologies, presented in table format.

pinyin-system.title_tr: Pinyin System: Initial Consonants and Final Consonants
pinyin-system.intro_tr: Pinyin (拼音[pīnyīn]) is the official romanization system that represents the pronunciation of Chinese characters using the Latin alphabet; it forms the foundation for learning correct sounds and tones before studying Hanzi. Each syllable typically consists of an initial consonant (声母[shēngmǔ], the consonant at the beginning of the syllable) and a final vowel (韵母[yùnmǔ], a vowel or vowel group), with a tone mark added above. Chinese has 21 initial consonants and approximately 36 final vowels; their combinations and four tones (plus neutral tone) make thousands of different syllables possible. In Pinyin, some letters are not pronounced as in Turkish (e.g., c, q, x, zh, r), so each sound must be learned separately. The tables below systematically summarize all initial consonants, final vowels, tone rules, and orthographic pitfalls.

The 'aspirated/unaspirated' distinction is a fundamental phonological difference in Chinese independent of tone: aspirated sounds (p, t, k, q, ch, c) have noticeable air release from the mouth.

tone-sandhi.title_tr: Tone Changes (变调 biàndiào): Rules for 不, 一, and Third Tone
tone-sandhi.intro_tr: In Chinese pronunciation, when certain syllables are placed next to each other, the pronunciation changes according to a rule called tone change (变调 biàndiào); this change only occurs during speech and is generally not shown in pinyin writing (except for 不 and 一, which are sometimes updated in the written form). The three most important rules are: (1) when two third tones are placed next to each other, the first one changes to the second tone, (2) 不 (bù) changes to the second tone (bú) before a fourth tone, (3) 一 (yī) remains in the first tone when standing alone, when used as an ordinal number, or when used with ten, but when placed before a first/second/third tone syllable it changes to the fourth tone (yì), and when placed before a fourth tone it changes to the second tone (yí). At HSK1 level, these rules immediately appear especially in very common patterns like 你好[nǐ hǎo], 不是[búshì], 一个[yíge], so memorizing them is necessary for accurate pronunciation. This page summarizes the three tone change rules separately and in table form with examples.

tables.caption_tr: Rule 1: Two Third Tones Side by Side (3rd tone + 3rd tone → 2nd tone + 3rd tone)
rows: gitmek istiyorum (yiǎng da 2. tona döner çünkü sonraki 3. tonla karşılaşıyor - zincirleme değişim)
footnotes_tr: The rule only affects pronunciation; pinyin writing is usually left with the original 3rd tone mark (ˇ).
When three or more 3rd tones are placed one after another, the rules are applied in a chain: they are usually grouped from end to beginning (e.g. 我很好 → wó hén hǎo).

tables.caption_tr: Rule 2: 不 (bù) Tone Change
footnotes_tr: 不 only changes before the 4th tone (falling tone); it always remains as bù before the other three tones.
Some dictionaries and textbooks update the pinyin writing to 'bú' when 不 appears before the 4th tone (such as bú shì, bú qù).

tables.caption_tr: Rule 3: 一 (yī) Tone Change
rows: Sıra sayısı (第一 vb.) veya sayının son hanesi
On sayısıyla (十一, 十一月ç vb.)
bir tane (个 nötr tondan türer, orijinali 4. ton gè)
footnotes_tr: 一 is the only syllable that can have four different pronunciations: yī, yì, yí, and sometimes neutral in context.
Rule summary: 一 + (1st, 2nd, 3rd tone) = yì; 一 + (4th tone) = yí; 一 alone, in ordinal form, or with ten = yī.

tables.caption_tr: Comparative Summary of Three Rules
rows: tek başına veya sonraki hece 3. ton değilse değişmez
1., 2., 3. ton veya nötr ton önünde, ya da tek başına
sıra sayısı, on ile birlikte, tek başına sayılırken
footnotes_tr: These three rules are the most frequently encountered tone changes at HSK1-HSK2 level; at advanced levels there are also 'yi' reduplication (yī yī) and some dialectal exceptions, but these are the basic rules.

yixia.title_tr: V + 一下 (yíxià): "To do something briefly/lightly"
yixia.intro_tr: 一下[yíxià] literally means "one time/one below," but when used immediately after a verb, it indicates that the action is done briefly, lightly, experimentally, or in a casual manner. It is very similar to Turkish patterns like "bir bak-ıver" (take a quick look), "bir dene" (try it), "azıcık dinlen" (rest a bit). It also softens imperative sentences, making them more polite and intimate; therefore it is used very frequently when making requests in Chinese. The structure is very simple: it is combined simply as "Verb + 一下[yíxià]," without any verb conjugation or additional rules. If it is to be used in the past tense, 了[le] is added immediately after the verb, before 一下[yíxià]: V + 了[le] + 一下[yíxià].

zui-superlative.intro_tr: 最[zuì] is an adverb in Chinese meaning "the most" and is a superlative degree marker, and it is always placed IMMEDIATELY BEFORE the adjective or verb it modifies; it almost perfectly corresponds to the "most" in English, therefore it requires no conjugation or additional structure. 比[bǐ] is used when comparing two things (A is more X than B), whereas 最[zuì] is used to indicate "the most X one among three or more things/people." It often appears with the 是...的 structure in the sentence ("it is the most X") or appears directly before the adjective as a predicate. Its negative form is constructed as 最不[zuì bù] + adjective/verb and carries a meaning like "the least/the worst" — there is NO usage in the form 不最. When the adjective comes after 最, there is no need for another degree adverb like 很[hěn], because 最[zuì] already indicates the highest degree.

suiran-danshi.intro_tr: "虽然[suīrán]...但是[dànshì]..." is the most common "although... but..." pattern in Chinese that connects two opposing ideas. The first clause (虽然) introduces a situation contrary to the expected result, while the second clause (但是) provides the actual result that occurs despite this expectation. It is very similar to the Turkish structures "although... but..." and "even though... yet..." but in Chinese both conjunctions are generally used TOGETHER (in the same sentence) — this is the point that Turkish speakers most often forget. 虽然 can be placed at the beginning of the sentence or immediately after the subject; 但是, on the other hand, is found at the very beginning of the second clause. This structure is one of the basic conjunctions at HSK2 level and is extremely frequently used in daily conversation.

footnotes_tr: Full sentence: 虽然他很累，但是他还在工作。(Although he is very tired, he is still working.)
In Chinese, 虽然 and 但是 are generally used TOGETHER; using only one does not seem natural as it would in Turkish.

yinwei-suoyi.intro_tr: The 因为...所以... [yīnwèi...suǒyǐ...] pattern is the most basic and most frequently used conjunctive structure in Chinese for establishing cause-effect relationships. 因为[yīnwèi] means "because, due to..." and appears at the beginning of the clause stating the reason; 所以[suǒyǐ] means "therefore, for this reason" and appears at the beginning of the clause stating the result. Although it resembles the Turkish "because... therefore..." structure, in Chinese -unlike Turkish- both conjunctions are generally used together in the same sentence. The reason clause (因为...) always comes first, the result clause (所以...) always comes second; this order is not flexible as it is in Turkish. In everyday speech, if the reason or result is already understood from context, one of the two conjunctions can be omitted.

tables.caption_tr: 因为...所以... Basic Structure
footnotes_tr: General rule: The reason clause starting with 因为 ALWAYS comes first, the result clause starting with 所以 ALWAYS comes second.

huozhe-haishi.title_tr: 或者 (huòzhě) vs 还是 (háishi): Two Different Uses of the Conjunction 'or'
huozhe-haishi.intro_tr: 或者 [huòzhě] and 还是 [háishi] are two conjunctions that mean 'or, or else' in Turkish, but their usage in different sentence types is completely different. 或者 is used ONLY in declarative sentences (陈述句 — sentences providing information or suggesting possibilities). 还是, on the other hand, is used ONLY in choice questions (选择疑问句 — 'A or B?' type questions). Using these two interchangeably is one of the most common mistakes made by foreigners learning Chinese; the rule is very simple: is the sentence a question or a declarative sentence? In sentences with 还是, moreover, 吗 is never added at the end of the sentence, because 还是 itself already creates a question.

li-distance.intro_tr: 离[lí] is a preposition (particle) used to express the DISTANCE (remoteness or proximity) between two points; it functions similarly to the Turkish suffixes "-den, -dan" but is only used when indicating distance/time intervals. Basic pattern: A + 离[lí] + B + (distance expression); meaning "A is this much far/near from B". 离[lí] does not require a motion verb, only indicates static distance between two points; therefore it should not be confused with the 从[cóng]...到[dào]... structure. Additionally, 离[lí] can also be used in time expressions to express "from now / until an event, how much time is left". The most important point for zero-level students is that 离[lí] as a subject takes not a PERSON but a PLACE or TIME POINT.

tables.caption_tr: 离[lí] Basic Structure: Expressing Distance (For Place)
rows: A + 离 + B + 有 + Mesafe

footnotes_tr: 很[hěn] does not carry the real meaning of 'very' here, it just appears obligatorily before the adjective (是 is not used).
多远[duō yuǎn] question pattern means 'how far'; answers typically use 很远/很近/不远/不太远.

tables.caption_tr: Expressing Time Intervals with 离[lí]

Yeni yıla sadece üç gün kaldı.
离 + Olay + 不远/很远了
lí ... bù yuǎn / hěn yuǎn le
footnotes_tr: In this structure 离[lí] refers to a TIME point, not place; the logic is 'there is A duration until event B'.

zai-progressive.title_tr: 正在 / 在...呢: Present Continuous (Ongoing Action)
zai-progressive.intro_tr: Chinese does not have a separate "present continuous" verb conjugation like in English; instead, to show that an action is happening at that very moment, 正在[zhèngzài], 在[zài] and the sentence-final particle 呢[ne] are used. These three elements can be used alone, in pairs, or in triple combinations; the meaning remains the same, only the emphasis changes. While the 正在...呢 combination gives the strongest and most explicit emphasis on "it's happening right now", using only 呢 carries a more colloquial and lighter tone. When forming the negative, 正在 and 呢 generally drop, replaced by simply 没(有)在. Since this structure will appear very frequently at HSK2 level, it is important to memorize all combinations and exceptions.

zai-vs-you.title_tr: 再 [zài] vs 又 [yòu]: The Difference of "Again"
zai-vs-you.intro_tr: 再[zài] and 又[yòu] are generally translated into Turkish with the same word, "again" or "once more," but in Chinese they cannot be used interchangeably. The fundamental difference between them is TIME: 再[zài] describes a repetition that has not yet occurred, is expected to happen in the future, or is desired (command, suggestion, plan, future); 又[yòu] on the other hand describes a repetition that has already happened, occurred in the past. Therefore, 再 is generally seen in command/request sentences and after verbs without 了, while 又 is generally seen in straightforward narrative sentences and mostly with 了 at the end of the sentence. Additionally, both have special patterns besides "again" (不再, 再也不, 又要...了, 先...再...) and these are shown in detail in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: The Basic Difference Between 再[zài] and 又[yòu]
rows: Emir, istek, öneri, plan, gelecek zaman
Düz anlatım, olmuş bir olayın aktarımı (geçmiş zaman)
Genellikle ALINMAZ (再 + V, 了 yok)
明天再来。 [Míngtiān zài lái.] (Yarın tekrar gel.)
他昨天又来了。 [Tā zuótiān yòu lái le.] (O dün yine geldi.)
没(有)再 [méi(yǒu) zài] = bir daha ...-madı (nadir, genelde 没 tek başına kullanılır)
footnotes_tr: The choice between 再 and 又 usually depends on the answer to the question 'has the event already happened, or not yet?'

tables.caption_tr: Commonly Used Patterns

我再也不去了。 [Wǒ zài yě bú qù le.] Bir daha asla gitmeyeceğim.
他又哭了。 [Tā yòu kū le.] O yine ağladı.
Yine ...-mek üzere (yaklaşan, çoğu zaman istenmeyen tekrar)
又要下雨了。 [Yòu yào xiàyǔ le.] Yine yağmur yağmak üzere.
先做作业,再玩游戏。 [Xiān zuò zuòyè, zài wán yóuxì.] Önce ödev yap, sonra oyun oyna.
她又漂亮又聪明。 [Tā yòu piàoliang yòu cōngming.] O hem güzel hem akıllı.

✓ 他昨天又来了。 [Tā zuótiān yòu lái le.]
Geçmişte gerçekleşmiş bir tekrar anlatılıyorsa 又 kullanılmalı, 再 değil.
✗ 请你又说一遍。 [Qǐng nǐ yòu shuō yí biàn.]

✗ 他再来了三次。 [Tā zài lái le sān cì.]

Geçmişte kaç kez olduğunu bildiren cümlelerde 又 kullanılır, çünkü olay(lar) zaten gerçekleşmiştir.

directional-complements-basic.title_tr: Foundations of Directional Complements (来/去, 上来/下去)
directional-complements-basic.intro_tr: Directional complements (方向补语[fāngxiàng bǔyǔ]) are suffixes that come after a verb and indicate the direction in which an action is performed. The most fundamental pair is 来[lái] (to come towards the speaker/listener) and 去[qù] (to go away from the speaker). These two words can be used independently, or they can combine with directional verbs such as 上[shàng], 下[xià], 进[jìn], 出[chū], 回[huí], 过[guò] to form compound directional complements like 上来/上去, 下来/下去, 进来/进去. The choice is determined entirely based on where the speaker (or the reference point of the narrative) is located: if the movement is toward the speaker, 来 is preferred; if the movement is away from the speaker, 去 is preferred. This topic covers the most basic patterns at HSK2 level; advanced compound directional complements that carry metaphorical/abstract meanings (起来, 下去's 'continue' meaning, etc.) are covered in a separate section.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Directional Complements: 来[lái] and 去[qù]
footnotes_tr: The reference point is always the speaker or the focal point of the narrative, not the listener.

tables.caption_tr: Complete Table of Compound Directional Complements (Directional Verb + 来/去)
footnotes_tr: The directional verb 起 combines only with 来; there is no pattern such as 起去.

de-degree-complement.intro_tr: 得 [de] (with soft pronunciation as "de") is a structural particle used to describe HOW/TO WHAT DEGREE a verb or adjective is realized; this is called a "degree complement" (程度补语[chéngdù bǔyǔ]). The structure is quite simple: Verb + 得 + Adjective (usually preceded by a degree adverb such as 很, 太, 非常). In Turkish expressions like "speaks very well", "runs fast", the adverb+verb relationship is created in Chinese by adding 得 to the END of the verb and then stating an adjective — it is the exact opposite word order from Turkish. Attention: This 得 is completely different in WRITING and MEANING from 的[de] (which indicates possession) and 地[de] (which forms adverbs); only their pronunciations (de) are the same. For verbs with objects (e.g., 说汉语), the verb must be REPEATED: 说汉语说得很好.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: Verb + 得 + Adjective
rows: Özne + Fiil + 得 + (很/太/非常) + Sıfat
Özne + Fiil + 得 + 不 + Sıfat
Özne + Fiil + 得 + Sıfat + 吗？
Özne + Fiil + 得 + Sıfat + 不 + Sıfat？
tā pǎo de kuài bu kuài
Özne + Fiil + 得 + 怎么样？
footnotes_tr: In affirmative sentences, 很 is mostly required; otherwise the sentence may carry a comparative meaning (e.g., 他跑得快 = can be understood as 'he runs faster than others').
In the negative, 得 remains; only 不 is added before the adjective; 得 is NEVER replaced with 不 (说不好 is a different structure — capability complement).

tables.caption_tr: Structure for Verbs with Objects (Verb Repetition)
rows: tā shuō Hànyǔ shuō de hěn hǎo
tā xiě zì xiě de hěn piàoliang
tā dǎ lánqiú dǎ de hěn hǎo
tā lánqiú dǎ de hěn hǎo
footnotes_tr: Rule: Verb + Object + Verb + 得 + Adjective.
Alternative: If the object is moved to the beginning of the sentence (after the subject), a single verb + 得 can be used without repeating the verb: 汉语她说得很好。

tables.caption_tr: Degree Adverbs Used Within 得
rows: 他跳得很好。 tā tiào de hěn hǎo
你说得太快了！ nǐ shuō de tài kuài le
她唱得非常好听。 tā chàng de fēicháng hǎotīng
你写得真漂亮！ nǐ xiě de zhēn piàoliang
他说得有点儿快。 tā shuō de yǒudiǎnr kuài
他跑得快极了。 tā pǎo de kuài jíle
footnotes_tr: 极了 is used AFTER the adjective, not before it: 好极了, 快极了.
Without these adverbs, if only 'Verb + 得 + Adjective' is said (without 很), the sentence generally carries a comparative / critical meaning.

tables.caption_tr: 得 / 的 / 地 Comparison (Same Pronunciation, Different Function)
rows: Derece tümleci (fiil/sıfat sonrası nasıl olduğunu bildirir)
footnotes_tr: All three are pronounced the same 'de' in speech; only the hanzi differ in writing.
Simple distinction tip: 的→BEFORE the noun, 地→BEFORE the verb, 得→AFTER the verb/adjective.

gei-coverb.title_tr: 给 (gěi) Preposition: Usage with the Meaning of '-e, For'
gei-coverb.intro_tr: The word 给 [gěi] is used both as a VERB meaning 'to give' on its own, and as a PREPOSITION (coverb) that adds the meaning '-e, for, on behalf of' when placed before another verb. When used as a preposition, the structure is as follows: Subject + 给 + Person + Verb (+ Object) — that is, 给 and the information about to whom it is done comes BEFORE the main verb. This structure appears very frequently with everyday verbs like 打电话 (to make a phone call), 写信 (to write a letter), 做饭 (to cook), etc. The most important point at HSK2 level is learning the POSITION of 给 in the sentence and not confusing it with other prepositions like 对/跟.

tables.caption_tr: Two Different Uses of 给: Verb or Preposition?
rows: 我给你一本书。[Wǒ gěi nǐ yì běn shū.]

Sana telefon ediyorum (senin için/sana yönelik arama).
Özne + 给 + Kişi + 送/买 + Nesne
他给我送了一本书。[Tā gěi wǒ sòngle yì běn shū.]
O bana bir kitap hediye etti.
footnotes_tr: When used as a preposition, 给 comes BEFORE the main verb; it performs the function that the '-e/-a' case suffix does in Turkish.

tables.caption_tr: 给 + Verb: Frequently Used Patterns
Position of 给 in the Sentence: Affirmative, Negative, Question
rows: 他给我打电话。[Tā gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà.]
Özne + 不 + 给 + Kişi + Fiil

Özne + 没 + 给 + Kişi + Fiil
他没给我打电话。[Tā méi gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà.]
Özne + 给 + Kişi + Fiil + 吗？
他给你打电话吗？[Tā gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà ma?]
Özne + 给 + Kişi + Fiil + 不 + Fiil
他给你打不打电话？[Tā gěi nǐ dǎ bu dǎ diànhuà?]
Özne + 给 + Kişi + Fiil + 了

footnotes_tr: Negation and question particles are NOT ALWAYS placed BEFORE 给; they are added to the beginning of the sentence (不/没) or at the end (吗); 给 maintains its position.

tables.caption_tr: 给 vs 对 vs 跟: Differences of Confused Prepositions

footnotes_tr: Rule: If the action REACHES someone or is done FOR someone's BENEFIT, 给 is used; if only FEELING/ATTITUDE about a topic/person is expressed, 对 is used.

yibian-yibian.intro_tr: The 一边[yìbiān]...一边[yìbiān]... pattern is used to express that the same person performs two actions AT THE SAME TIME and corresponds to the Turkish expression "while... while..." The structure is formed by placing 一边[yìbiān] before both verbs: Subject + 一边[yìbiān] + Verb1 + 一边[yìbiān] + Verb2. The subject of both actions must necessarily be the same person/people; this pattern cannot be used for two different subjects. It is generally used with short, everyday verbs (eating, talking, listening, walking, etc.) and is very frequent in spoken language. At HSK2 level, it is sufficient to learn this pattern with only two verbs (一边...一边...); there are advanced-level variants for three or more actions.

le-completed.intro_tr: 了 (le) is a very important aspect particle in Chinese used to indicate that an action has been completed or has occurred. Unlike the past tense suffix in Turkish (-dı/-di), 了 does not indicate the TIME of the verb, but rather the COMPLETION of the action; therefore it can be used in past, present, and even future completed actions. It typically comes immediately after the verb (V+了+Object), and if the object is modified by a specific number, measure word, or adjective, the sentence becomes more natural. In negative sentences, 了 is completely dropped and replaced by 没(有) — this is one of the most common mistakes made by beginner-level students. 了 also has a different usage at the end of sentences to indicate a change of state; on this page the main focus is on 了 after the verb for "completed action".

tables.caption_tr: The Basic Position of 了 and Sentence Structure
rows: Wǒ mǎi le sān běn shū.
Fiil + 了 + Nesne + 了 (cümle sonu, devam eden durum)
Wǒ chī le sān ge píngguǒ le.
Şimdiye kadar üç elma yedim (belki devam edecek).
Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Hànyǔ.
footnotes_tr: If the object is a bare (indefinite/general) noun, 了 alone does not complete the sentence; the continuation of the sentence is needed: 我吃了饭就走。(I left as soon as I ate.)

tables.caption_tr: Negative and Question Forms
rows: Özne + 没(有) + Fiil + Nesne (了 DÜŞER!)
Özne + Fiil + 了 + Nesne + 吗？

ordinal-di.intro_tr: Creating ordinal numbers in Chinese ("first, second, third...") is very easy: you simply add the prefix 第[dì] before the cardinal number. Unlike Turkish, there is no separate suffix system — 第[dì] always stays the same, only the number after it changes. 第[dì] is generally used with a measure word (个, 次, 本 etc.) or directly with a noun. The most important point to note is that the number "two" in ordinal form is always expressed with 二[èr]; 两[liǎng] is NEVER used in ordinals. This structure appears very frequently at HSK2 level: class/lesson order, floor numbers, competition rankings, and phrases like "the first time" are all constructed with this pattern.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Basic Ordinal Number Formation with 第 (dì)
footnotes_tr: The rule is fixed: 第[dì] + [Cardinal Number]. No matter how large the number is, the structure does not change.

tables.caption_tr: 2. 第 + Number + Measure Word + Noun Structure
footnotes_tr: 第[dì] can be used directly with a noun (第一课), a measure word is not required, but when counting people/objects, it is more natural to add a measure word (第一个人).
For the question "Which ordinal?" use 几[jǐ] within the 第 pattern: 第几?

tables.caption_tr: 3. Comparison of Cardinal Numbers with Ordinal Numbers
rows: 第一 miktar değil, sıra bildirir
第二 (ikinci) — 两 DEĞİL, 二 kullanılır!
⚠️ 第两 YANLIŞTIR; her zaman 第二 denir
İkiden büyük sayılarda asal/sıra aynı karakteri paylaşır
Onlar basamağında da 二 kullanılır, 两 değil
footnotes_tr: This is the most common mistake students make: '两' is only used when counting quantity/objects (两个人), it is NEVER used when indicating ordinal number.

guo-experience.title_tr: 过 (guo): Experience Aspect — "...have the experience of doing"
guo-experience.intro_tr: 过 [guo], added after a verb to indicate that an action in the past was EXPERIENCED/LIVED AT LEAST ONCE; it corresponds to the Turkish pattern "gitmişliğim var, yemişliğim var" (I have the experience of going, I have the experience of eating). It is not important whether that situation currently continues or not, only the information "this experience happened in my life" is conveyed. 过 always comes immediately after the verb, before the object, and is toneless (read lightly). Negation is never done with 不, but with 没 or 没有, and in this case 过 remains in the sentence (没去过, NOT "不去过"). At HSK2 level, the most confused topic is the difference with 了 [le]: 了 emphasizes a completed/finished action, while 过 emphasizes an experience in the past.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Sentence Structure: Affirmative, Negative, Question
rows: 我没(有)去过中国。[Wǒ méi(yǒu) qùguo Zhōngguó.]
你去过中国吗？[Nǐ qùguo Zhōngguó ma?]
你去过中国没有？[Nǐ qùguo Zhōngguó méiyǒu?]
footnotes_tr: 过 comes immediately after the verb, before the object if present: Verb + 过 + Object word order does not change.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of 过 (guo) and 了 (le)
rows: Genelde yok; sadece 'bu bir kez oldu' bilgisi verir
Genelde var; sonucu şu anı etkiler
没(有) + Fiil + 过 (过 kalır)
我学过法语。[Wǒ xuéguo Fǎyǔ.] — Fransızca öğrenmişliğim var (şu an bilmeyebilirim)

Zero seviyede ikisini ayrı ayrı öğrenmek yeterlidir
footnotes_tr: The most practical rule at beginner level: if answering the question 'have I ever done it?', use 过; if giving the information 'I did/finished it', use 了.

le-change-of-state.intro_tr: Sentence-final 了[le] is a particle that indicates a situation was PREVIOUSLY different but is NOW changed, or entering a new stage; it corresponds to meanings like "now," "has happened," "entered" in Turkish. This 了[le] is added to the very END of the sentence, not immediately after the verb, but to the end of the entire sentence, and is generally seen in sentences with nominal, adjectival, or stative predicates. While verb-final 了[le] indicates the COMPLETION of an action, sentence-final 了[le] indicates a CHANGE OF STATE — these two can sometimes overlap in the same sentence. The easiest tip for beginner-level students: if you can add a word like "now," "has happened," or "entered/came" when translating the sentence into Turkish, there is likely a need for sentence-final 了[le]. This page summarizes patterns and exceptions in table form.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Sentence-final 了[le] — Basic Examples of Change of State
rows: 我是老师了。 [Wǒ shì lǎoshī le.]
现在不下雨。 [Xiànzài bú xià yǔ.]
我还没有钱。 [Wǒ hái méiyǒu qián.]
我有钱了。 [Wǒ yǒu qián le.]
她不会说汉语。 [Tā búhuì shuō Hànyǔ.]
她会说汉语了。 [Tā huì shuō Hànyǔ le.]
footnotes_tr: 了[le] is always added to the very END of the sentence, not immediately after the verb.
In adjectival predicate sentences, 是[shì] is not used; the adjective serves directly as the predicate (see the 很/是 page).

tables.caption_tr: 2. Frequently Used 了[le] Patterns
rows: 要下雨了。 [Yào xià yǔ le.]
我不去了。 [Wǒ bú qù le.]
V + 了 + 数量 + 了
我学了三年了。 [Wǒ xuéle sān nián le.]
Hâlâ devam eden süre: '3 yıldır öğreniyorum (ve devam ediyor).'
Aşırılık vurgusu: 'Çok/fazla pahalı!' (durum değişikliğinden çok pekiştirme)
你吃饭了吗？ [Nǐ chīfàn le ma?]
你还在学校吗？ [Nǐ hái zài xuéxiào ma?]
Durumun devam edip etmediğini sorar (karşılaştırma için)
footnotes_tr: If two 了[le] are used together in the 数量+了 pattern (verb-final + sentence-final), it indicates that the action is still ongoing.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Comparison of Sentence-final 了 vs Verb-final 了

Cümlenin en sonunda: 吃饭了 [chīfàn le]

他吃饭了。 [Tā chīfàn le.] — Yemek yedi (artık yemiş durumda / yeni bilgi).
Çok yaygın: 他高了。 [Tā gāo le.]
没(有) + fiil, 了 düşer: 没吃饭 [méi chīfàn]
不...了 kalıbı: 不吃了 [bù chī le] (vazgeçme)

tables.caption_tr: 4. Negation: Two Different Meanings of 不...了

bu-vs-mei.title_tr: 不 [bù] vs 没 [méi]: The Difference in Negation
bu-vs-mei.intro_tr: In Chinese, two basic words are used for negation: 不[bù] and 没[méi] (abbreviated as: 没有[méiyǒu]). These two words are not interchangeable; the difference between them is too important to be covered by a single Turkish negation suffix "değil/-me/-ma". In short: 不[bù] negates the present tense, future, habits, general facts, and subjective wishes/judgments (with verbs like 是, 想, 要, 会, 应该); 没[méi], on the other hand, negates actions that did not occur in the past or have not yet been completed, and negates the verb "有" (to have/there is). The most critical rule: it is never used together with 了[le] — when an action is negated with 没, the 了 in the sentence completely disappears. This page clarifies which negation should be used in which context using tables.

measure-words-common.title_tr: Common Measure Words (本, 张, 杯, 件, 只...)
measure-words-common.intro_tr: When counting a noun in Chinese, a 'measure word' (量词[liàngcí]) must always be placed between the number and the noun; similar to the words 'tane' and 'adet' in Turkish expressions like 'bir tane kitap, iki adet araba', but in Chinese every noun category has its own specific measure word that varies according to the noun. The most general and 'wildcard' measure word is 个[gè] and can be used in uncertain situations, but 本[běn] for books, 张[zhāng] for flat objects, 件[jiàn] for clothing, 只[zhī] for animals, and similar more correct choices are preferred. The choice of measure word is generally determined by the shape of the object (long-thin, flat, round), its container (cup, bottle, bowl), or its category (person, animal, building, vehicle). This structure is mandatory not only with numbers, but also with 这[zhè]/那[nà] demonstrative pronouns and 几[jǐ]: number/demonstrative + measure word + noun. The tables below summarize the most commonly used measure words, usage patterns, and frequently confused pairs.

bi-comparison.intro_tr: 比 [bǐ] is the most basic and most frequently used preposition in Chinese for comparing two things; it corresponds to the "than" structure in English. The basic logic is simple: 比 [bǐ] is placed between the two elements being compared, followed by an adjective (or some verbs), and the meaning of "more" is already embedded in 比 [bǐ] itself, so adverbs indicating "very/extremely" such as 很 [hěn], 非常 [fēicháng] SHOULD NOT be used before the adjective. To specify how large the difference is, at the end of the sentence can be added 一点儿 [yìdiǎnr] (a little), 得多/多了 [de duō / duō le] (much more) or before the adjective 更/还 [gèng/hái] (even more). For the negative form of comparison, instead of 比 [bǐ], the 没有 [méiyǒu] structure is used; for equality, the 跟...一样 [gēn...yíyàng] structure is used. This page summarizes at a glance all the basic patterns of 比 [bǐ], its negative and equality forms, and the most common mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Comparison Structures with 比 [bǐ]
rows: 他比我高。tā bǐ wǒ gāo.
A + 比[bǐ] + B + Sıfat + 一点儿[yìdiǎnr]
他比我高一点儿。tā bǐ wǒ gāo yìdiǎnr.
A + 比[bǐ] + B + Sıfat + 一些[yìxiē]
这个比那个便宜一些。zhège bǐ nàge piányi yìxiē.
A + 比[bǐ] + B + Sıfat + 得多[de duō]
今天比昨天冷得多。jīntiān bǐ zuótiān lěng de duō.
A + 比[bǐ] + B + Sıfat + 多了[duō le]
这个比那个贵多了。zhège bǐ nàge guì duō le.
A + 比[bǐ] + B + 更/还[gèng/hái] + Sıfat
他比我更忙。tā bǐ wǒ gèng máng.
A + 比[bǐ] + B + Sıfat + Sayı + Birim
他比我大三岁。tā bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
footnotes_tr: In 比[bǐ] sentences, degree adverbs such as 很[hěn], 非常[fēicháng], 太[tài] SHOULD NOT be used before adjectives; the meaning of "more" is already contained in 比[bǐ].
更[gèng] and 还[hái] emphasize that both things already have that quality, but one has more of it.

tables.caption_tr: Negative Comparison and Equality Structures
rows: A + 没有[méiyǒu] + B + (那么/这么[nàme/zhème]) + Sıfat
我没有他那么高。wǒ méiyǒu tā nàme gāo.
A + 不如[bùrú] + B + (那么[nàme]) + Sıfat
这个不如那个好。zhège bùrú nàge hǎo.
Bu ondan iyi değil (o daha iyi).
A + 跟/和[gēn/hé] + B + 一样[yíyàng] + (Sıfat)
我跟他一样高。wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo.
A + 跟[gēn] + B + 不一样[bù yíyàng]
我的想法跟你的不一样。wǒ de xiǎngfǎ gēn nǐ de bù yíyàng.
A + 不比[bù bǐ] + B + Sıfat
弟弟不比哥哥矮。dìdi bù bǐ gēge ǎi.
Küçük kardeş büyük kardeşten kısa değil (aynı boyda ya da daha uzun olabilir).
footnotes_tr: The 没有[méiyǒu] structure is NOT the direct negative of 比[bǐ]; it carries the meaning of "not as... as", meaning A is less/lower in degree than B.
不比[bù bǐ] means "A is not less/lower than B"; it generally carries a tone of defying expectations, and 没有[méiyǒu] is preferred for simple negation.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Corrections

affirmative-negative-question.intro_tr: The V不V (Verb-不-Verb) structure is the most natural way to ask yes/no questions in Chinese and is the most commonly used form in spoken language. The verb (or adjective) is stated in its affirmative form, and immediately afterwards its negative form is repeated with 不[bù]; this creates a meaning like "are you going or not going?" but is generally translated into Turkish simply as "...-yor musun?" (are you...?). This structure is actually the complete equivalent of a question formed with the question particle 吗[ma] (去吗?), but in V不V question sentences, 吗[ma] is NEVER used — the two never occur together. In disyllabic verbs and adjectives, one must pay attention to the abbreviation rule; furthermore, since the negative form of the verb 有[yǒu] is not 不有 but 没有[méiyǒu], this verb is specially asked as 有没有[yǒu méiyǒu]. This topic is a basic and very frequently encountered pattern at HSK2 level.

tag-questions.title_tr: Affirmative Questions (好吗?, 是吗?, 对不对?)
tag-questions.intro_tr: In Chinese, affirmative/verification questions like "isn't it?", "is that so?", "okay?" in Turkish are formed by adding a small "particle" (tag) to the END of a sentence. The most common particles are 好吗?, 是吗?, 对吗?, 对不对?, 好不好?, 行吗? and 可以吗?. The structure is very simple: first a normal sentence (plain statement, no question particle) is spoken, then the particle is added after a comma — the rest of the sentence doesn't change at all. Which particle to use depends on whether the question is "to verify a fact" (是吗?/对吗?/对不对?) or "to get approval for a suggestion/permission" (好吗?/好不好?/行吗?/可以吗?). This structure is different from asking a question by putting 吗 in the sentence; because here the truth or acceptability of an already established statement is being questioned.

你去过北京，是吗？[Nǐ qùguo Běijīng, shì ma?] — Pekin'e gitmiştin, öyle mi?
Somut bir bilginin/gerçeğin doğruluğunu sormak için
今天星期五，对吗？[Jīntiān xīngqīwǔ, duì ma?] — Bugün Cuma, doğru mu?
对吗?'nin daha vurgulu, konuşma dilindeki hâli (V-不-V yapısı)
你叫王明，对不对？[Nǐ jiào Wáng Míng, duì bu duì?] — Adın Wang Ming, değil mi?
好吗?'nin V-不-V yapısıyla söylenişi, öneri onayı

Bir eylemin uygun/kabul edilebilir olup olmadığını sormak
我明天再还你，行吗？[Wǒ míngtiān zài huán nǐ, xíng ma?] — Yarın sana geri veririm, olur mu?
我拍张照，可以吗？[Wǒ pāi zhāng zhào, kěyǐ ma?] — Bir fotoğraf çeksem, olur mu?

cong-dao.intro_tr: The 从...到... [cóng...dào...] pattern corresponds to the "from...to" structure in Turkish and expresses the distance between two points, a time interval, or a change. 从 [cóng] indicates the starting point, and 到 [dào] indicates the ending/arrival point; they are always used in this order in the sentence, first 从 then 到. This pattern can be used for place (space), time, numbers, and abstract concepts (transition from one state to another). 从 and 到 can also be used separately if needed: 从 alone means "from", and 到 can function both as a postposition ("to") and as a verb ("to arrive"). The 从...到... phrase usually appears after the subject and before the verb.

Saat dokuzdan ona kadar ders var.

verb-reduplication.intro_tr: Verb reduplication in Chinese is formed by repeating a verb to express that an action is short-term, light, casual, or done "for the purpose of trying"; it corresponds to expressions in Turkish such as "let me take a look", "rest a bit", "try it out". Monosyllabic verbs are reduplicated in the form AA (看看), A一A (看一看) or in the past A了A (看了看), while disyllabic verbs are reduplicated in the form ABAB (讨论讨论) — it should not be confused with the AABB pattern in adjectives. This structure softens the action, makes the request more polite/comfortable and is generally used in daily spoken language, in sentences expressing suggestions, requests or attempts. Reduplicated verbs cannot be negated and generally come before the object if there is one; the second syllable is often pronounced with a light (neutral) tone.

de-shihou.intro_tr: The ...的时候[de shíhou] pattern means '...-when' or '...-while' in Turkish and is used to indicate during which time period an event occurs. The structure is very flexible: a verb phrase, an adjective, a noun, or a complete clause (subject + predicate) can precede it. 的[de] here functions like a possessive/attributive particle, while 时候[shíhou] means 'time' or 'moment'; together they mean 'the time of...' or 'the moment when...'. In sentences, the 的时候[de shíhou] phrase typically appears at the beginning of the main clause (functioning as a time adverbial), but sometimes it can also come after the verb. This is a fundamental temporal conjunctional structure frequently encountered at HSK2 level and is one of the patterns that should be memorized from beginner level onward.

In the 小时候 pattern, 的 is often omitted; it is called '小时候' directly, and '小的时候' is used less frequently.

zhe-continuous.intro_tr: 着 [zhe] is an aspect particle that is added immediately after a verb and generally does not have the 4th tone, but is read with a light (neutral) tone; it imparts a meaning close to Turkish expressions like "...-mış/-miş durumda", "...-arak". It has two main uses: (1) to indicate that a CONDITION resulting from an action continues to exist (門開著 = the door is standing open), (2) to indicate that two actions occur SIMULTANEOUSLY, with one showing how the other is done (its manner) (笑著說 = said with a smile). Additionally, it is frequently used in EXISTENCE sentences that describe what is located somewhere using the pattern "Place + V著 + Object" (牆上掛著一幅畫 = a picture is hanging on the wall). 着 never changes its position: it always comes immediately after the verb, before the object; its negative is formed with 沒(有), and it is not used together with 了.

Olumsuz Emir: 别/不要 + V + 着
footnotes_tr: 着 is never used together with 了 in the same verb: 開了著 (WRONG).

footnotes_tr: 着 and 正在 can be used together: expressions like 他正在穿着大衣 are natural, but generally 正在 alone emphasizes the ongoing nature of the action, while 着 emphasizes the permanence of the result.

duo-questions.title_tr: 多 (duō) + Adjective Questions (多长, 多高, 多远)
duo-questions.intro_tr: The word 多 (duō) combines with monosyllabic adjectives to form measurement/degree questions meaning 'how...?'; patterns like 多长[duōcháng] 'how long', 多高[duōgāo] 'how tall', 多远[duōyuǎn] 'how far' are the most frequently used. This structure is used to numerically learn about the physical characteristics (length, height, weight, age, distance, duration) of an object or person. Generally, it is constructed with the subject + 有[yǒu] + 多 + adjective pattern, but in some patterns like 多大[duōdà] (asking age), 有[yǒu] is not used. Answers are given in the form of number + measurement unit + adjective, for example 三米高[sān mǐ gāo] 'three meters tall'. This topic is basic grammar at HSK3 level and is indispensable for asking about height, distance, weight, and duration in daily life.

de-three-way.title_tr: Comparison of 的 / 得 / 地 — Distinguishing the Three 'de' Particles
de-three-way.intro_tr: In Chinese, three different characters (的, 得, 地) are read in exactly the same way as 'de', which is why it is one of the most confusing grammar points for beginner-level students. However, they have completely different functions in writing, and choosing the correct character is important for the sentence to be comprehensible. In short: 的 attaches to a noun (possession/attribution: answers the question 'whose' or 'what kind of'), 地 attaches to a verb and comes before it (adverb: describes 'how' the action is performed), and 得 comes after a verb or adjective and clarifies the degree or result of that action. The easiest way to distinguish these three is to look at what the character comes BEFORE or AFTER in the sentence: 的 before a noun, 地 before a verb, 得 after a verb/adjective. The tables below summarize all the usage patterns of these three particles and common mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: Comparison of the Three 'de' Particles

我是坐飞机来的。[wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de]

tables.caption_tr: 地 [de] — Adverb Formation Uses
rows: 高高兴兴地说 [gāogāoxìngxìng de shuō]
Tek heceli sıfat: genelde 地 kullanılmaz
慢慢, 静静 vb. + 地 + Fiil

他说汉语说得很好。[tā shuō Hànyǔ shuō de hěn hǎo]
Fiil/Sıfat + 得 + 要死/不得了/慌
